notes: Account summary: large logistics SaaS provider building live chat and automated reranking for routing decisions.
Primary ask: dedicated capacity with throughput guarantees and clear autoscaling behavior for bursty peaks (weekday mornings).
Targets discussed: steady-state 800-1200 RPS for short text chat API; p95 latency target 90-150ms depending on model; simultaneous 1500 concurrent sessions during peak promotions.
Capacity planning: prefer reserved GPU pool with burst buffer; exploring 24/7 warm pool sized at 15-25% of committed capacity to reduce cold-starts.
Scale-up policy preference: aggressive scale-up on queue depth + sustained CPU/GPU utilization above 70% for 30s window; scale-down conservative with cooldown 5-10min to avoid thrash.
Warm pool behavior: pre-warm containers on pinned GPUs, keep KV caches warmed for top-10 flows; trade-off conversation around cost vs tail latency improvements.
Queueing behavior: want bounded queue with back-pressure to clients and retry guidance; ask for token-level rate limiting and prioritized routing for SLA customers.
Fallback and graceful degradation: must support automatic fallback to q4 quantized variant with deterministic routing policy and monitored quality regression alerts.
POC metrics observed: cold-start median 20s, warm-request p95 ~95ms; batching improved throughput but increased p95 by ~10ms at low concurrency.
Cost sensitivity: moderate — willing to pay premium for predictable p95 guarantees but want clear credit model for SLA breaches and option for reserved vs variable bursting.
Security: VPC-only control plane path, KMS for key material, SOC2 proof requested and ISO27001 is a plus. Data residency in US-East required for subsets of traffic.
Quotes from CTO: 'Need deterministic tail latency, not just average numbers — burst windows break our routing rules today.'
Notes on SLA negotiation: legal asked to define burst window length, credit calculation (tokens vs request), and permitted maintenance windows.
Internal Redwood asks: provide warm-pool sizing spreadsheet, sample SLA language for throughput guarantees, and historical 6-month infra availability stats.
Suggested Redwood configuration: reserved pool (commit) sized for baseline 800 RPS, surge pool billed at fixed per-GPU hourly rate, warm pool 20% of commit, canary rollout 10% traffic.
Decision criteria: if POC can demonstrate p95 <=120ms with warm pool enabled and <1% tail SLA violations over 7 days, procurement moves to contract.
Commercial asks from Keystone: flexible commit tiers (3,6,12 months), rollback/escape clause for model degradation, integration with their internal observability (Grafana export)
Next technical concerns: precise definitions for 'warm' state, expected cache hit ratios, and how KV cache warming behaves across restarts.
Jira escalations: RED-4281 captured request for detailed cold-start repro steps and required mitigations; INF-3320 tracking warm-pool cost modeling
requirements_summary: Throughput guarantee: contractual baseline 800 RPS with burst to 1500 RPS for promotional windows
Latency SLOs: p95 <= 120ms for warm requests, p95 <= 300ms overall including cold starts (negotiable)
Reserved GPU planning: baseline committed GPUs + surge pool; request examples for 8x A100 equiv shapes
Autoscaling: scale-up on queue depth + util windows, scale-down with 5-10min cooldown, support for scheduled scale events
Warm pools: 15-25% of committed capacity, KV cache pre-warm for top flows, ability to define warm thresholds
Queueing: bounded queue with client back-pressure and prioritized lanes for mission-critical requests
Fallbacks: deterministic model fallback path to quantized variant with rollback hooks and eval monitors
Observability: token-level latency, per-route SLO charts, export hooks to customer Grafana and audit logs
